newsitem.title: THAILAND: Sumitomo upbeat on Thailand despite woes.
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo upbeat on Thailand despite woes.

text.p: Thailand's current economic problems are overblown and natural for an economy undergoing deep structural change, the general manager of Sumitomo Bank Ltd's Thai unit said on Monday.

"Thai people have not experienced a turndown in the economy like this in the past and people are responding too much... Thailand is now trying to adapt to a different style of economic growth," Kozo Yoneda told Reuters in an interview.
Confidence in the Thai economy has been hit by a number of concerns including sharply slowing growth, a large current account deficit and sluggish exports in 1996.
Authorities earlier this month forced the finance sector, savaged by more than 800 billion baht ($30.8 billion) in loans to the depressed property sector, to undergo a major revamp.
Ten weakened finance firms were asked to boost their capital and all financial institutions were told to raise provisions for sub-standard loans, mainly given to the property sector.
Yoneda said the growing gap between economic growth and the development of social institutions and physical infrastructure that supported growth was causing Thailand difficulties.
Slower economic growth would allow these structures to advance and ensure transition to more stable growth, he added.

Thailand's economy grew 6.7 percent in 1996, its lowest rate for a decade and down from 8.7 percent growth in 1995. Central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond said recently that economic growth this year will be around 6.8 percent.
"In the past, growth has been too fast, infrastructure, human resources and social structures couldn't catch up with the economic growth," he said.
Education had been a particular problem and had caused a shortage of skilled labour, Yoneda added.
"There are many workers in Thailand but not enough middle class people. There are not many middle class technicians, accountants or lawyers," he said.

"I am still very positive on the future of the Thai economy. It's a matter of comparison. Among Asian countries, Thailand still offers lots of opportunities and I think it is then natural that Japanese banks like Sumitomo will concentrate our business efforts in Thailand," he said.
Thailand gets more than 40 percent of its foreign investment from Japan. Outside Japan, the Thai market is Sumitomo's third most significant in Asia after Hong Kong and Singapore, he said.

Sumitomo Bank's Thai branch has a total loan portfolio of around $5.7 billion, of which some $1.7 billion was "out-in" lending through the bank's offshore Bangkok International Banking Facilty operation in which money is borrowed offshore for relending in Thailand, Yoneda added.

Some 70 percent of the bank's loans were to Thai corporations and demand in infrastructure, automobiles, steel, petrochemical, agriculture and brewing industries was expected to see loan growth at 30 percent this financial year, he said.
The bank's clients include several major Thai corporations including parts of the giant Charoen Pokphand group, state-owned Thai Oil, auto makers and others, Yoneda said.
Sumitomo was recently awarded branch status in Thailand.
